name: Yusuf Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time for this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, and your name never goes with your answers. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the workshop lead at Brennan's Garage on Canal Street, four bays, mostly older cars and the vans of local builders and plumbers. I open up at half seven, check the job cards on the board, and give the two younger lads their jobs before I start on whatever nobody else can crack. This week it's a gearbox on a twelve-year-old van that whines in third. I love that part, the listening and the feeling for it. What wears me out is the phone ringing and people wanting a price before I've even lifted the bonnet.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You said nobody else can crack some jobs. What does that look like on a normal week?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Most weeks there's one car that's been to two other garages first. The dealer plugged it in, got a fault code, swapped a part, and it's still broken. I put my hand on the engine, take it for a drive, and nine times out of ten it's something simple like a split vacuum pipe. Pat (my boss) jokes that I'm the garage's last resort, and honestly I'm proud of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say, which is that a computer can't hear a bearing going. At the garage we'd have a laugh about it, because Pat (my boss) already got sold a fancy booking app that nobody used. Online I don't post much, but I'd share something about how the real problem is car makers locking us out of their software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means I'm fine on the AI side. My worry was never the robots, it was the car makers making every repair go through the dealer. If AI fizzles, that fight is still there, and it's the one that actually squeezes garages like ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do, and keep putting a bit away each month like Ines (my partner) and I already do. We've got about four months of bills saved and want to get to six by next summer. I'd maybe push Pat to pay for the electric car course, because more of those are turning up and I've been avoiding them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty relaxed about the AI part, if I'm honest. There's a bit of a knot about the electric cars, because I'm good at engines and that's what's going away slowly. But that's a ten-year thing, not a next-month thing.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You said you've been avoiding the electric cars. What's behind that?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the money got tight at the garage in this world, what would go first at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Partly it's just that I don't know them and I hate not knowing something in front of the lads. Partly it's the voltage, you get it wrong and you're dead, not just embarrassed. I'm the best gearbox man on Canal Street, and in ten years nobody will have a gearbox for me to fix.

say: A **computer can't hear** a worn bearing, so this hype was never going to replace a good mechanic.
The real fight is **car makers locking** independent garages out of their repair software.
think: My job is **safe from AI** here, and I always thought it would be.
The slow **switch to electric** cars is the thing that actually threatens my skills.
do: Keep running the workshop and **saving monthly** until we reach **six months** by next summer.
Ask Pat to pay for the **electric car course** I've been putting off.
feel: **Relaxed** about AI itself, with a small **knot** about electric cars slowly replacing engines.
S0.quote: I'm the best gearbox man on Canal Street, and in ten years nobody will have a gearbox for me to fix.
fieldNote: He measures his worth by **fixing what others can't**, and that pride shapes everything he says.
His real fear is **electric cars**, not AI, and he admits he's been dodging the training.
Blames **car makers** and dealers, not technology itself, which fits his left-leaning view on big firms.

steps.text: Keep leading the four bays at Brennan's Garage as normal
Save until the joint fund covers six months of bills
Ask Pat to fund the electric car safety course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good luck to the AI getting under a rusty van in the rain. At work I'd probably moan that it's the front desk jobs that go first, and that's not fair on the people doing them. Online I'd back anyone pushing for rules so firms can't just sack people and pocket the savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it worries me more than I'd say out loud. Half my edge is the thinking bit, working out what's wrong, and if a cheap AI does that from the fault codes, then any kid with a spanner can follow its list. Pat (my boss) would pay for the kid and the subscription, not for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay put, because I don't know where else I'd go that's any better. I'd stop spending on the motorbike I've been doing up and keep that money in savings. I'd also talk to the other senior mechanics in town about whether there's an association we can join, because on our own we've got no voice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like the ground going a bit soft under me. Not falling, just soft. I'm 27 and I thought I'd picked a trade that was safe for life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the garage would you worry about in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Who at the garage would you worry about in this world?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a fault code is often wrong. What happens if customers start trusting an AI over you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carol on the front desk first, she does bookings and quotes and that's exactly the stuff on your list. Then probably me, which is strange to say. If an app tells a nineteen-year-old apprentice what's wrong with the van, the garage doesn't need a twenty-seven-year-old on senior pay.

say: AI won't get under a **rusty van** in the rain, whatever the tech firms claim.
Front desk staff will **lose out first**, and firms shouldn't pocket the savings without rules.
think: Half my value is **working out faults**, and that thinking part is exactly what AI takes.
Pat would rather pay an **apprentice plus an app** than keep me on senior pay.
do: Stop spending on the **motorbike project** and put that money into savings instead.
Talk to other senior mechanics in town about joining a **trade association** together.
feel: Like the **ground going soft**, not collapsing but no longer the safe trade he chose.
S1.quote: If an app tells a nineteen-year-old apprentice what's wrong with the van, the garage doesn't need a twenty-seven-year-old on senior pay.
fieldNote: He sees clearly that the **diagnosis part** of his job is thinking work and could be split off.
Worries first about **Carol** on the front desk, then admits he could be next himself.
Resistant to change, so his plan is **staying put** and finding strength in numbers, not new skills.

steps.text: Pause spending on the motorbike rebuild and bank that money
Gather senior mechanics in town to join a trade association
Stay on at Brennan's Garage rather than look elsewhere

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly I'd say this is what happens when nobody regulates tech firms, and the government needs to step in now. At work I'd tell the lads we'll be fine because cars still need hands for a while. I'd be signing every petition going, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, it means the clever part of my job is gone in two years and the spanner part in five. I'm not good with computers, I've never touched these AI tools, and I'd be learning all of it from behind. By 2031 I'm 32 with no plan B.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything. No holiday, no motorbike, Ines and I would stop eating out and try to get to a year of savings instead of four months. I'd go to every meeting of any union or association that'd have me. I'd look at jobs that need a body in the room longer, maybe roadside breakdown or the council's fleet yard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. Like when a car you've worked on for two days comes back with the same fault and you don't know why.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Ines that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Ines (my partner) that her job caring for old people is safer than mine now, which would be a funny thing to say out loud. Then I'd probably go quiet and sit in the garage at home. Ines (my partner) is a care worker, and for the first time in our lives her job looks safer than mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the hands-on part buys you three years. What would you do with those three years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use them to save and to find out what job keeps a person in it longest. I keep thinking breakdown work, out on the roadside at two in the morning, because nobody's sending a robot to a lay-by in the sleet first. But I'd be guessing, I really don't know.

say: This is what happens when **nobody regulates** tech firms, and government must act right now.
Cars still need **hands for a while**, so the lads at the garage will be fine for now.
think: The **diagnosis side** goes in two years and the **spanner side** in five.
I've never used AI tools, so I'd be **learning from behind** with no plan B at 32.
do: Cut holidays, eating out and the bike to build **a year of savings** with Ines.
Join **any union** or mechanics' association that will take him and attend every meeting.
Look at **roadside breakdown** work or the council fleet yard, where hands stay needed longer.
feel: **Sick**, like a repaired car coming back with the same fault and no idea why.
S2.quote: Ines (my partner) is a care worker, and for the first time in our lives her job looks safer than mine.
fieldNote: He works out the **three-year gap** between AI and robots himself and sees it as a short reprieve.
The moment his partner's **care job looks safer** than his is clearly a shock to him.
Wants government to **regulate**, but has no personal plan beyond saving and guessing at breakdown work.

steps.text: Cancel the holiday and stop eating out with Ines
Build joint savings from four months to a full year
Attend every meeting of a mechanics' union or association
Apply for roadside breakdown or council fleet yard jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so let's use them properly, with retraining money from the government and not just leaflets. At the garage I'd tell Pat (my boss) we need a plan. Online I'd say the companies making these things should pay into a fund for the people they put out of work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is better, but for me it lands at the same place, just at 35 instead of 32. The diagnosis work goes in 2031 and the hands-on in 2034. I'd at least have time to get the electric car ticket and maybe something else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd finally do the high-voltage course and keep saving. I'd join the association and push for a training fund. And I'd start asking around about the council fleet yard, because a public job with a pension feels safer than a little garage that might close.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still uneasy in my stomach, but less sick. It's like getting a warning light early instead of the engine seizing on the motorway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the first of those five years look like for you, practically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Practically, the first year is the electric course in the spring and saving every month. I'd keep my hours at Brennan's and maybe do Saturdays at the fleet yard to get my foot in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said you hate not knowing things in front of the lads. Would that stop you learning the new tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would slow me down, I won't pretend it wouldn't. I'd probably learn the tools at home first, where nobody can see me fumble. I'd rather look stupid in my own kitchen for a month than look stupid in front of the apprentices for a year.

say: Five years is enough time **to retrain**, if government puts real money in, not leaflets.
The companies building this should pay into a **fund for workers** they put out of work.
think: The end point is the same, just at **35 instead of 32**.
Five years gives me time for the **high-voltage ticket** and maybe a second skill.
do: Take the **high-voltage course** next spring and keep saving every month.
Do **Saturday shifts** at the council fleet yard to get a foot in a public job.
Learn the **new tools at home** first, away from the apprentices' eyes.
feel: Still **uneasy** in the stomach, but less sick, like a **warning light** that comes on early.
S3.quote: I'd rather look stupid in my own kitchen for a month than look stupid in front of the apprentices for a year.
fieldNote: The extra years let him **plan concrete steps**, though the end point still scares him.
Pride is a real barrier: he'd **learn in private** so the apprentices don't see him struggle.
Looks to a **public job with a pension** as the safe harbour, which fits his politics.

steps.text: Take the high-voltage electric car course next spring
Push the mechanics' association for a government training fund
Work Saturdays at the council fleet yard to get hired there
Keep saving every month toward a year of bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this fairly, so there's no excuse for leaving people behind. At work I'd tell the lads to get their electric tickets now. Online I'd push for training paid for by the firms that profit, same as the other times.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years feels like a long time when you're 27. Robots wouldn't be in the garage until 2039 and I'd be nearly 40. That still scares me a bit, because 40 is young to be starting over, but it's not tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the electric course, keep saving, and stay at Brennan's. In a few years I'd see if the council fleet yard has a proper job going. I wouldn't jump at anything, that's not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more like the normal worry you'd have anyway. Ten years is long enough that I'd probably end up doing what my dad did, which is complain and then get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years from now you'd be 37. What does a good version of that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A good version is me as the lead at the fleet yard, with a pension, still with my hands on engines most days. Ines and I would own a little house by then, I hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change anything for you and Ines beyond work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We've talked about kids, maybe in five years or so. With ten years' warning I think we'd still have them, just later and with more saved. With ten years' warning, Ines (my partner) and I would still have kids, just later and with more money in the bank.

say: Ten years is **enough to be fair**, so there's no excuse for leaving workers behind.
Firms that profit should **pay for training**, and the lads should get electric tickets now.
think: Robots arriving around **2039** means starting over close to **40**, which still scares me.
Ten years feels long at 27, so it's **not tomorrow**.
do: Do the **electric car course** and keep saving while staying at Brennan's Garage.
Apply for a **council fleet yard** job in a few years, without rushing.
feel: **Ordinary worry**, the kind he'd feel about work anyway, eased by the long runway.
S4.quote: With ten years' warning, Ines (my partner) and I would still have kids, just later and with more money in the bank.
fieldNote: Even with a decade, the idea of **starting over at 40** keeps him from feeling secure.
His ideal future is a **public job** with a pension, hands still on engines.
Family plans hold: **kids later**, with more saved, rather than not at all.

steps.text: Finish the electric car course while staying at Brennan's
Keep monthly savings going toward a house deposit
Put off having children with Ines for five years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, no contest, because there's no time to do anything except panic quietly. What would help is a proper paid course, run in the evenings, with someone patient who doesn't make you feel thick. And a law that says car makers have to share repair software with garages like ours.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask who's going to fix the robots. Everyone assumes they'll fix themselves. Somebody still has to change the oil in the robot that changed my oil, and I'd like that somebody to be me.

headlineQuote: Somebody still has to change the oil in the robot that changed my oil, and I'd like that somebody to be me.
portrait: **Yusuf** is a 27-year-old workshop lead at Brennan's Garage, proud of fixing **what others can't**.
He's never used **AI tools** and dreads learning anything new in front of the apprentices.
His deeper fear is **electric cars** making his gearbox and engine skills slowly worthless.
He blames **car makers and tech firms**, and wants regulation, retraining funds and a union voice.
He moves from **uneasy** in the plateau to **alarmed** when AGI comes in two years.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most, because there's no time to prepare before the diagnosis work goes.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid evening course** with a patient teacher who doesn't make him feel thick.
A **law forcing car makers** to share repair software with independent garages.
